title: DC motors and gears
about: Why robots need gearboxes: trading speed for strength.

html: A DC motor spins whenever electricity flows through it.

Inside, a coil of wire becomes a magnet when current flows through it. Magnets around the coil push and pull it, so it spins. Little metal brushes keep switching the current so it keeps turning.

• More volts: it spins faster.
  • Swap the two wires: it spins the other way.
Fast but weak
A small motor spins thousands of times a minute (rpm means turns per minute). But its torque, its twisting strength, is tiny. Hook it straight to a wheel and a robot can't even climb a small ramp.
A gearbox fixes that. A small gear on the motor turns a bigger gear on the wheel. With a 20:1 gearbox, the motor turns 20 times for every 1 turn of the wheel, so the wheel:

• turns 20 times slower
  • pushes about 20 times harder (a little less, because gears rub)
Big ratios like 50:1 use several pairs of gears in a row.
When a motor stalls
If the load is too heavy, the motor stops turning. That's called a stall. A stalled motor pulls the most electricity it can, and all that energy turns into heat. Leave it stalled and it can burn out.
So engineers pick the gear ratio carefully: enough torque that it never stalls, but not so much gearing that the robot crawls.

steps.q: A motor spins at 6,000 rpm. It drives a wheel through a 20:1 gearbox. About how fast does the wheel turn?
steps.explain: The motor turns 20 times for each turn of the wheel: 6,000 ÷ 20 = 300 rpm.

steps.q: Your robot stalls halfway up a steep ramp. What's the best fix?
options: Use more gearing, like 50:1 instead of 5:1
steps.explain: More gearing gives the wheels more torque, so the robot can climb. It goes slower, but it gets there.
The wheel turns slower but pushes harder. That's the trade-off.
